analysis.one_liner: Combines a higher minimum wage, police accountability rules, gun limits, rent relief, and tax hikes on wealth into one omnibus.
analysis.headline: Introduced in September 2020 with 46 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was referred to 18 House committees and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This was a catch-all civil rights and economic package covering jobs, policing, gun policy, housing, health care, and education. It would raise the federal minimum wage, ban most evictions temporarily, expand the child tax credit and SNAP, raise the estate tax and capital gains rates, end step-up basis at death, remake policing (qualified immunity, a misconduct registry, use-of-force standards), decriminalize marijuana with expungement of past convictions, and cut student loan costs. It died without any committee or floor action.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-wage workers (a higher minimum wage), Black families and other communities of color (economic development, health equity, civil rights enforcement), renters (a refundable rent credit, an eviction moratorium, tenant protections), people experiencing homelessness, student borrowers (loan relief and lower Parent PLUS costs), people with criminal records (expungement, fair-chance hiring), and victims of gun and domestic violence.

how_it_helps.text: Title I raises the federal minimum wage, phases out the subminimum tipped wage, and bans salary-history discrimination in hiring [S3].

Division B includes the George Floyd Justice in Policing Act: qualified immunity reform, a national police misconduct registry, use-of-force standards, a ban on no-knock warrants in drug cases, and restrictions on chokeholds and the transfer of military equipment to police [S3].
The marijuana provision decriminalizes cannabis, expunges past convictions, and opens Small Business Administration programs to cannabis businesses [S3].
Title IV creates a refundable rent credit, a temporary moratorium on eviction filings, homelessness funding, and lead-safe housing requirements [S3].
Title III raises the child tax credit for families under 150% of poverty, adds summer SNAP benefits for children, and funds a federal job guarantee pilot [S3].
Division A would restore school infrastructure bonds and grants to rebuild public schools, and Title V expands Pell Grants and allows student loans to be discharged in bankruptcy [S3].
The tax side pays for some of it by raising the capital gains rate, taxing capital gains at death or gift, and modifying the estate tax rate and exclusion [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The highest-income households (estate tax and capital gains changes), gun manufacturers and dealers (liability lawsuits restored, background checks on all sales, trafficking and ammunition limits), brand-name drug makers (anti-delay provisions to speed cheaper generics), police departments and unions (new liability and reporting rules), landlords (eviction moratorium and tenant blacklisting ban), and the federal treasury overall.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wealthy estates, gun makers, drug makers

drawbacks.text: It is a multi-trillion-dollar omnibus spanning at least 18 committee jurisdictions, introduced late in an election year with no cost estimate or scoring in the record, and many titles are studies, commissions, or task forces rather than enacted programs [S2][S3][S5].

The tax offsets fall entirely on concentrated wealth, which guaranteed intense opposition from that side, and the eviction moratorium and ban on police in schools would impose real costs on small landlords and local school districts [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Most of the package directs benefits to low- and middle-income households and would be paid for largely by taxes on large estates and capital gains. The honest objections are design, not direction: it bundles dozens of unrelated bills into one vehicle too large to deliberate, its costs are not offset in the record, and several provisions would have needed serious negotiation (particularly policing liability and immigration detention rules) to become law.

outcome.mechanism: The Speaker referred it to 18 House committees the day it was introduced; no committee ever marked it up and no floor vote ever happened, so it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Karen Bass introduced the Jobs and Justice Act of 2020 on September 23, 2020, with 46 Democratic cosponsors, all members of the Congressional Black Caucus [S1][S4].
The bill was referred to 18 House committees at once, a structure that splits a bill into pieces no committee owns and usually signals it is a message bill rather than a vehicle for action [S5].
Only five Transportation and Infrastructure subcommittees took referrals; no committee held a markup, no vote was scheduled, and the bill died when the Congress ended January 3, 2021 [S5].

Several of its major pieces had already passed the House as standalone bills during the same Congress (the George Floyd Justice in Policing Act and the MORE Act), but this combined package was never brought to the floor [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the highest-income households kept current estate and capital gains tax treatment, gun manufacturers kept their liability shield, brand-name drug makers kept pay-for-delay tools, and police departments avoided new liability and reporting mandates. Low-wage workers, renters, and communities the bill targeted for investment gained nothing from this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wealthy estates, gun makers, drug makers, police

sides.party_line_note: All 46 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican supported it; no roll-call votes were ever taken, so no formal party split exists in the record.

industries.note: The bill repeals the industry's federal liability shield, requires background checks on every sale, restricts trafficking, straw purchases, and online ammunition sales, and raises the minimum purchase age for certain rifles. The current liability shield is what has largely insulated the industry from lawsuits over gun violence.

Anti-pay-for-delay provisions curb settlements that keep cheaper generics off the market, close loopholes around 180-day exclusivity, and ease sample access for biosimilar makers. Cheaper generic competition directly lowers what patients and insurers pay.

Qualified immunity reform, a national misconduct registry, decertification requirements, mandatory use-of-force reporting, and bans on chokeholds and no-knock drug warrants would create accountability tools citizens currently lack. The industry's interest in avoiding liability runs against the public's interest in redress for misconduct.

Raising the capital gains rate, taxing gains at death or gift (ending step-up basis), and modifying the estate tax would raise taxes concentrated at the very top, partially funding the bill's programs.
Federal decriminalization removes criminal exposure and opens SBA lending and services to the industry, while expungement addresses the racial imbalance of prior enforcement.
The RESCUE Act title codifies the Minority Bank Deposit Program and directs deposits and regulation toward Black and community banks, expanding lending access in underserved neighborhoods.

Medicaid expansion incentives, territory Medicaid funding, and marketplace stabilization provisions route more public coverage dollars through private insurers, expanding coverage while locking the industry in as the delivery channel.
A temporary eviction moratorium and a ban on tenant blacklisting restrict landlord remedies, while a refundable rent credit channels public money to landlords for tenants' rent.
